slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Hi everyone, welcome. I am Julie. If you came because an ad promised something impressive and you are thinking, wow, she looks very normal: I am very normal. That is the whole point. 2023: second place in the Rejuvenation Olympics, out of hundreds. People around me on the leaderboard spent small or large fortunes; I did it on a gym membership, a short supplement list and the best vegetables and meat I can buy. Structural engineer by training: skeptical, I became the scientist and the experiment for 25 years. Disclosure: affiliation with NOVOS; everything else I personally use. Personal experience, not medical advice.

slides.title: Why
slides.notes: Square one: why did I do any of this? Not a leaderboard. It started in pain, 26 years ago. As a single mom, watching my brother die suddenly, I knew I was my son’s plan and his back-up plan. Now he is 20: I want to be here for grandkids and show him another possibility for how we age. That is the vision I run to. The reality I run from: dementia, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, the silent decade of decline. It hit my family. I wanted a dashboard: a way to test whether my choices were moving the needle.

slides.title: The test
slides.notes: The test I and many aging scientists settled on: DunedinPACE. It estimates the speed your body is aging. 1.0 means one year per calendar year. My best score was 0.65; the average of my three tests is 0.665. So I age about 6.5 years while the typical person ages 10. Built at Duke and Columbia from the Dunedin, New Zealand cohort followed since birth; published 2022; used in 65+ large studies in 18 countries. Nature Aging 2024: faster pace predicted shorter healthspans and lives. The part ads leave out: my score went back up to 0.76 after supplement mistakes and a chaotic menopausal stretch. Testing again at year end. One test, one person, one body: a story, not a clinical trial.

slides.title: The cake
slides.notes: Why did the world get obsessed with longevity? Aging is the biggest risk factor for the four things we fear: heart disease, cancer, dementia, type 2 diabetes. Slow aging itself and you push all four back at once. That is the bet of geroscience. Here is how I organize it: longevity is like a cake. Four layers: sleep, food, movement, stress management. That is where the work lives. For women, one thin layer at the bottom: peri and post menopause. Then the icing: sauna, peptides, stem cells, light therapies, the gadgets and supplements all over your feed. Icing is delightful. Nobody ever ate a bowl of icing and called it a good cake.

slides.title: The icing
slides.notes: Why start with the icing? Because it is everywhere and makes people feel behind. Affordable on the left: sauna, prebiotics, most supplements. Real money as you move right: NAD drips, peptides, stem cells, hyperbaric oxygen, rapamycin. At the far end a program costing about two million dollars a year with a medical team and blood transfusions. I am not saying don’t. I am saying not first. Nobody in the blue zones is in a hyperbaric chamber. What I do: a tested longevity supplement combination and sauna three to five days a week; the sauna is what gets me out of bed. Finnish data 2024: 2,575 men, 28 years; four to seven sessions a week, about 40 percent lower all-cause mortality than once a week. The coin on the far left is me: twelve dollars a day.

slides.title: Menopause
slides.notes: Before we bake, one thing that gets filed under icing by mistake: menopause therapy. For half the room, menopause will change sleep, bones, mood, appetite, energy, body shape. It changes how well every other layer can do its job: perfect sleep hygiene cannot beat hot flashes. If you are doing everything right and the scale still moves up, it is not simply eat less, move more. The Menopause Society position, 2022: for healthy symptomatic women under 60 or within ten years of menopause, benefits generally outweigh risks. November 2025: the FDA removed the black-box warnings. The only action: find a clinician who specializes in hormone therapy, look for the letters MSCP. HRT has been great for me and is not right for my sister. No hormones because of a webinar.

slides.title: Sleep
slides.notes: Bottom of the cake: sleep, the night shift. Your brain has a drainage system that flushes the day’s waste, mostly while you sleep: the glymphatic system, imaged in living people for the first time by OHSU in 2024. No middle-of-the-night shame spirals; I have had insomnia. Focus on what we control: timing and routine. 2023, 60,000-plus adults: sleep regularity predicted lifespan better than duration; the most regular sleepers had up to 48 percent lower mortality risk. My routine: last meal three hours before bed, ten-minute walk, screens off an hour before, brush, floss, wash, eye mask, cool room. Target window 9 PM to 5 AM. Borrow the order and the consistency, not my clock.

slides.title: Quote
slides.notes: For anyone who lives by this line: you will die much earlier by it as well. I used to admire it. Then I started testing. The fastest way to speed up your pace is neglecting sleep. Be consistent. Everything else we cover tonight will help your sleep inside that window.

slides.title: Food
slides.notes: Take the type of diet off the table. Vegan, keto, Mediterranean, carnivore: I have done them; I call them try-its. Take the religion out of your diet. Four universal pillars. One, fiber variety: a diverse microbiome is one of the clearest signatures of healthy aging. Two, protein adequacy: muscle is your longevity savings account; anabolic resistance means more quality protein per meal as we age. Three, polyphenol and micronutrient density: eat the rainbow; deeply colored vegetables, dark berries, greens, olive oil, green tea, coffee. Four, minimal ultra-processed food. My plate: a pound of vegetables a day, half greens; wild blueberries or pomegranate daily; one gram of protein per pound of lean mass; a ten-hour eating window. It took years. Start slowly or your gut will make you regret it.

slides.title: Sugar
slides.notes: Sugar and glycemic stability. What we subtract matters as much as what we add. Three words: spike, signal, scar. Spike: what the monitor shows after sugar or simple carbs. Signal: a flood of insulin; locked on high all day, your cells become a garage that never gets cleaned out; chronic over-signaling is a hallmark of aging. Scar: glycation; sugar cross-links collagen and elastin; wrinkles are the visible proof, arteries, eyes and kidneys the invisible one. HbA1c measures sugar stuck to protein. UCSF 2024: 342 women around forty; every gram of added sugar came with an older biological age; they averaged 61 grams a day. BMJ review: keep added sugar under 25 grams, about six teaspoons. Birthday cake stays. Confession: pizza barely moved my monitor; my greens latte spiked it. Every Academy student wears a monitor for two weeks.

slides.title: Same age
slides.notes: Third layer: movement. One picture of why it matters: two people, the same age in calendar years. One strong, one on a walker. Mayo Clinic, December 2024, 183 countries: the gap between how long we live and how long we live in good health. Worldwide 9.6 years. United States 12.4 years, the widest gap in the world. I am in the middle of this with my parents: a decade of not getting to the store or the bathroom alone, losing email and the phone, forgetting finances and grandchildren, falling at night. Not everything is escapable. But exercise is the single most powerful intervention we have. Can we shrink that window to almost nothing? What movement?

slides.title: Movement portfolio
slides.notes: I think of exercise like an investment portfolio. One stock is not diversified, it is optimistic. Four areas. Weights: resistance training, compound lifts; for muscles, bones and increasingly the brain. VO2 max: how much oxygen you can use working hard; declines with age even in elite athletes; hard intervals plus recovery; for heart and lungs. Zone 2: conversational-pace cardio, walking, hiking; metabolic health and heart. Mobility and balance: full range of motion and steadiness; for the brain and the safety to keep doing the other three. Runners add weights and mobility; lifters add cardio and yoga. Data: grip strength tracks mortality almost in a straight line across 48 studies and three million people. 7,000 steps versus 2,000: 47 percent lower mortality, 38 percent lower dementia; not ten thousand. Mayo 2024: the one-leg stand fell fastest with age. Tonight: shoes off, non-dominant leg, aim for thirty seconds.

slides.title: Movement week
slides.notes: That is what my week looks like. How do you fit all this in? I did not build it in a day: twenty-five years of adding, subtracting and fine-tuning. Travel and deadlines change it, but the bones stay. It is an example of a diversified portfolio, not a test to pass tomorrow. Start small: short movement breaks, a few sets of air squats through the day, cut post-meal glucose spikes by over twenty percent; big leg muscles pull glucose straight out of the blood. A daily walk and air squats while the coffee brews is a very respectable start. Check with your doctor if you need to. The goal is to start moving.

slides.title: Stress
slides.notes: The fourth layer is the one almost everyone skips. I hate the phrase stress management; it sounds like an HR seminar. But stress is the silent saboteur: pristine diet, all the weights, 7,000 steps, and elevated cortisol undoes it from the inside. 2018, a stressful divorce: my cortisol curve was inverted, rock bottom in the morning, spiking at night. Supplements are a band-aid. I learned Transcendental Meditation; six months later the curve had normalized and has stayed that way. TM is not magic; breathwork, mindfulness, prayer, meditation all trigger the same reset. The best practice is the one you will do. Free five-minute tool: the physiological sigh, Stanford: five minutes a day improved mood and calmed the nervous system faster than standard meditation. Double inhale through the nose, long slow exhale through the mouth. Three together, now.

slides.title: The protocol
slides.notes: All four layers in a single day, so you can see where they fight for the same hour. 5 AM wake, water, prayer, light. 7 AM movement and sauna. 8 AM eating window opens: greens, protein, fiber, fruit. 9 AM caffeine cut-off. Eating window 8 to 6, ten hours: constraining eating to 8 to 10 hours improved blood sugar and body fat without changing what people ate; earlier windows do even better. Midday main meal and a walk. 1 PM stress reset. 6 PM kitchen closes, three hours before bed. 8 PM screens off. 9 PM lights out. Notice: the whole day is built backward from bedtime. Lights out at nine sets dinner at six; dinner at six sets the window opening at eight. Sleep is the master foundation. Life wins sometimes; I reset the next morning. What transfers is the order of operations: sleep, then food, movement, stress. My 5 AM might be your 6:30. Screenshot this slide and pick one or two anchors.

slides.title: Test then buy
slides.notes: Tracking does not have to be expensive. Almost every layer shows up in a number you can measure with a pencil, a notebook, a modest watch or scale: steps, resting heart rate, sleep duration, blood pressure. The goal is to stop guessing. Supplements: the best advice is not a list. My stack is tailored to my body, genetics and blood work; yours should be too. Work with your physician or a functional medicine doctor to see your baseline: vitamin D, homocysteine, inflammatory markers, micronutrients. Test first, then targeted buying. A blood test tells you where the cake has a hole so you know where to put the icing. What I take, as one example: D3 with K2; magnesium taurate, malate and glycinate; B-complex; omega-3s; NOVOS, which I have an affiliate account with. Full breakdown at JulieGibsonClark.com. Inside the Academy we walk through this with your own labs in front of you.

slides.title: Three questions
slides.notes: That is the cake. Numbers are not what kept me showing up for twenty-five years. Three questions did. Intention: the sentence on the wall. Mine: I want my healthspan to match my lifespan; drag the second line up to meet the first. Why: the feeling behind it, the engine that keeps you going when protocols become routine. Mine: being here to show my son a different possibility for how we age, and keeping Parkinson’s and dementia far away. Resources: time, energy, money, relationships, the real amounts. Mine: about an hour in the morning and twelve dollars a day. Resources filter out the adverts. No million-dollar budget? Great: let go of peptides and stem cells and focus on a solid gym routine. Friends who want this too? Start a group. When all three align you stop asking what should I do and start asking does this fit. A sauna session fits. A 9 PM bedtime fits. Not willpower: three honest questions doing the heavy lifting.

slides.title: Welcome. I am very normal.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 1 · 2:00
Welcome. I am very normal.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

An ad promised something impressive and now the room is looking at a normal woman. She is normal. That is the whole point. Second in the world in 2023, on about twelve dollars a day, while the people around her on the list spent small fortunes. She is an engineer; she became the scientist and the experiment.

THE ONE IDEA

A normal person, an extraordinary number, almost no money. The whole hour lives in the gap between those two facts.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

She is the picture. The slide must not compete with her face, so there is no object. A navy field lit from behind, and then the two facts arrive one after the other, as large as anything in the deck: "Second in the world, 2023" in cream, "About twelve dollars a day" in light blue. Nothing else. The restraint is the design: the room reads the two numbers, looks back at her, and the contradiction does the work her words are doing.

BUILT WITH

Typography only. Two builds. The light behind the field is the only motion.

slides.title: Why I went down this path.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 2 · 2:00
Why I went down this path.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Nobody wakes up wanting to be on a leaderboard. She is a single mom; for most of her son's life it has been the two of them. She wants to be the mother who can still carry the groceries at seventy and still hold a conversation at ninety. She watched someone she loves age faster than they should, and the question stopped being "will it happen to me" and became "how fast, and what can I do."

THE ONE IDEA

Her why has a face. This is the only slide in the hour that is allowed to be personal before it is scientific.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

Her script asks for one photograph, full bleed, graded into the navy, headline low and left, nothing moving. That photograph is hers to give: her and her son, or her alone. A generated picture here would be a lie in the one place the hour cannot afford one. Until she sends it, the slide carries her two ages instead: 70 and 90 as the two largest numbers on screen, with her two lines beneath them, "carry the groceries" and "hold a conversation". The numbers make the why concrete without inventing a face.

BUILT WITH

Her photograph when it arrives. Until then, the two ages in Playfair, cream and light blue, on the lit field.

slides.title: Ten years pass. By this test, I age about six. The speed towards death.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 3 · 1:30
Ten years pass. By this test, I age about six. The speed towards death.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

For every ten calendar years her body has aged about six, by this test. Most people age ten. The test is DunedinPACE; scientists call it pace of aging, she calls it the speed towards death because it is the same thing and harder to ignore. 1.0 means one year per year. Her best was 0.65, her three-test average 0.665, and the honest part the ads leave out: it went back up to 0.76 and she is testing again in December.

THE ONE IDEA

Everyone in the room is moving toward the same place; the only question is how fast. She found the speedometer.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

Three builds, in her order. First the plain line alone, huge, so the room gets the point before any science. Then the speedometer she drew herself: a dark glass instrument, 1.0 at the top labelled "most people", the needle on 0.665 in light blue, the small tick at 0.76, the right side of the dial running into red toward "faster than the calendar". Every number is engraved into the face of the instrument, part of the object, not laid over a photo. Third, the population curve rises beside it: most people bunched at 1.0, a tail aging fast, and one marked point at 0.665. The gauge says what she measures; the curve says where she sits among everyone else. Both are needed, because the speed means nothing without the crowd.

BUILT WITH

The instrument is built as a real object in code, so the labels are part of the dial: brushed rim, dark glass, engraved ticks, a glowing needle. The curve is drawn, with her point lit. DunedinPACE, Belsky et al., eLife 2022; Balachandran et al., Nature Aging 2024.

slides.title: Longevity is like a cake.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 4 · 1:30
Longevity is like a cake.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Aging is the biggest risk factor for the four things everyone fears: heart disease, cancer, dementia, type 2 diabetes. Slow the aging itself and all four move back at once; that is geroscience, and that is her bet. Then her picture: the cake is four things, sleep, food, movement, stress management, where most of the work lives. One more thin layer for the women in the room. The icing is sauna and the expensive therapies. Nobody has ever eaten a bowl of icing and called it a cake.

THE ONE IDEA

Four layers do the work. The icing is on top for a reason: it comes last and it holds nothing up.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

First build, small and plain: one root, four branches. Aging at the root, the four diseases on the branches. Second build: the cake, whole, hero size, every layer lit evenly this once, labelled exactly as she drew it: Sleep at the bottom, Food, Movement, Stress Management, the thin layer beneath them, the icing labelled Therapies. It is a real cake, baked and iced, because she is a baker and the metaphor only works if the room wants to eat it. It returns at the start of every layer with that layer lit, so the cake becomes the map of the whole hour.

BUILT WITH

The whole uncut six-layer cake, photographed; the layer labels sit beside it with leader lines, not on it. The geroscience tree is drawn. Buck Institute; López-Otín et al., Cell 2023.

slides.title: Not wrong. Not first.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 5 · 5:30
Not wrong. Not first.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

She starts with the icing because it is everywhere and it makes people feel behind. She is not saying don't; she is saying not first. The whole spectrum on one slide: affordable on the left, sauna, prebiotics, most supplements; real money on the right, NAD drips, peptides, stem cells; rapamycin, a prescription and a doctor; and at the far end the two-million-a-year program. Nobody in the blue zones is in a hyperbaric chamber. Four things she would leave alone until the cake is baked. Her own icing: the sauna, three to five days a week, the one piece of icing with twenty-eight years of data behind it, and the reason she gets out of bed. And the coin at the far left: twelve dollars a day, mostly groceries.

THE ONE IDEA

Price and proof are two different axes. The expensive end of the room is not where the evidence is.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

A map, not a list: cost left to right, strength of human evidence bottom to top. Each therapy is a marker placed where it belongs, so the room sees in one glance that sauna sits cheap and high, the drips and peptides sit expensive and low, rapamycin sits in the middle with a doctor beside it, and the two-million program is off the edge. Four markers turn amber when she names them. The sauna marker warms when she tells the sauna story. The coin lands last, bottom left. The map carries the whole argument of the block: order, not prohibition.

BUILT WITH

A drawn chart with real axes and large labels, the markers lit, on a white panel so it reads as evidence, not decoration. Sauna data: Kunutsor et al., Scand. Cardiovasc. J. 2024; Laukkanen et al., BMC Medicine 2018. Placements to confirm with her.

slides.title: Menopause therapy is a layer, not icing.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 6 · 2:30
Menopause therapy is a layer, not icing.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

One thing gets filed under icing by mistake, usually by people who have never been through it. For half the room, menopause changes sleep, bones, mood and body, and it changes how well every other layer can do its job. Decoration does not do that; this is a thin layer of the cake. The Menopause Society's 2022 position: for healthy symptomatic women under sixty or within ten years of menopause, benefits generally outweigh risks. In November 2025 the FDA removed the black-box warnings. The action is one line: find a doctor through the Menopause Society. Then the bridge: four layers hold up the cake.

THE ONE IDEA

This belongs in the cake, not on it. And there is a window.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

The cake returns with everything dark except the thin layer, lit. That is the entire first build: the room sees the layer she means. Second build: a short timeline, menopause to ten years after, with the window highlighted, because the science she quotes is a window and the slide should look like one. The line beneath: The Menopause Society, find a certified practitioner. Final build: the four layers light bottom to top, the icing dims, and the headline changes to "Four layers hold up the cake", which is the sentence that starts the next forty-five minutes.

BUILT WITH

The cake photograph, masked so only the thin layer is lit. The timeline drawn. Menopause Society 2022; FDA, November 2025.

slides.title: Sleep is the repair shift.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 7 · 4:00
Sleep is the repair shift.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Sleep is when the body does its maintenance while she is not in the way, and that is not a metaphor: the brain's drainage channels were imaged in living people for the first time in 2024. Regularity predicted who lived longer better than duration, in sixty-one thousand people; the most regular sleepers had up to a forty-eight percent lower risk of dying. Her exact numbers: lights out at nine, up at five, last meal three hours before bed, screens off an hour before, cool and dark. Borrow the order, not her clock.

THE ONE IDEA

Night is a shift with a schedule, and the same bedtime every day matters more than the hours.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

The cake with sleep lit, for her first sentence. Then the night arc: 9 PM on the left, 5 AM on the right, moon to sun, one arc of light across a dark sky, with a band across the deepest part of the night labelled "the repair shift". Her five numbers are the only type, placed along the arc where they happen: last meal at six, screens off at eight, lights out at nine, up at five, eight hours between. The arc turns her rules into a single shape the room can picture tonight at 8:45.

BUILT WITH

The arc rendered as a night sky from moon to sunrise; the band and the five numbers placed on the arc as part of the model, with the sky kept dark where the type sits. Windred et al., Sleep 2023; Piantino et al., PNAS 2024.

slides.title: "I'll sleep when I die," said the person aging at twice the normal speed.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 8 · 1:00
"I'll sleep when I die," said the person aging at twice the normal speed.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

She used to admire the line. Then she started testing.

THE ONE IDEA

The joke everyone makes is the test result everyone fears.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

Nothing but the line, cream on the lit navy, the largest type since the two facts. No object. A beat of silence before she speaks. The slide is a pause with a punchline; any picture would soften it.

BUILT WITH

Typography.

slides.title: Take the religion out of your diet.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 9 · 5:00
Take the religion out of your diet.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Vegan, keto, Mediterranean, carnivore: it is not about the type. Look at the plate. Protein is the floor, there at every meal. Fiber is the lever: the target is 25 to 38 grams and more than ninety percent of women and ninety-seven percent of men miss it, so almost everybody has room. Whole food is the default. Her rules: a pound of vegetables a day, a gram of protein per pound of goal weight, eating between eight and six, coffee cut at ten, zero alcohol on training days. Not a word about weight, on purpose.

THE ONE IDEA

Stop arguing about the religion and look at the plate: three parts, five numbers.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

The cake with food lit, for the opening. Then one plate, seen from above, real food, divided into its three parts: protein as the floor, fiber as the lever, whole food as the default, one line each. Final build: her five numbers around the rim of the plate, like the hours on a clock. Beside the plate, two numbers that make the fiber point land: 25 to 38 grams, and 90 percent of women who miss it. A plate because that is her word and her unit; the numbers on the rim because the rim is where she puts them in her head.

BUILT WITH

A top-down plate, photographed, the three parts real; the lines and the five numbers placed around it, not on the food. Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020 to 2025.

slides.title: The one thing every diet agrees on.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 10 · 5:00
The one thing every diet agrees on.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Every diet disagrees except on this: sugar is bad for aging. The model in three words. Spike, what a glucose monitor shows after a sugary meal. Signal, what the spike switches on: insulin and the nutrient-sensing pathways, and when they are on all day that is one of the twelve hallmarks of aging. Scar, the part people don't know: sugar sticks to proteins, glycation, and HbA1c is literally sugar stuck to red blood cells. UCSF, 2024: every gram of added sugar came with an older biological age. BMJ: under 25 grams a day. Her confession: pizza barely moved her monitor; the healthy green drink spiked her.

THE ONE IDEA

Sugar is not a calorie problem. It spikes, it signals, and it scars, and you can measure all three.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

One object, the glucose trace from a monitor like the one every Academy student wears: a sugary meal as the sharp spike, a balanced plate as the low wave beside it. The three words sit at the three moments of the object: Spike at the peak; Signal as the band beneath the curve that stays lit after the spike has fallen; Scar at the tail, where the HbA1c number lives. The trace is hers in spirit, the green drink that spiked her. Final build: the object dims and two large checkboxes appear, Move dinner earlier and Rebuild one plate, under "Your two Monday changes", because that is how the sleep and food half of the hour ends.

BUILT WITH

The trace drawn as a monitor would draw it, the signal band and the scar mark part of the chart. Chiu, Epel and Laraia, JAMA Network Open 2024; Huang et al., BMJ 2023; López-Otín et al., Cell 2023.

slides.title: Same age.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 11 · 2:00
Same age.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

She is not demonstrating a workout. One picture of why movement matters: two people, the same age, one standing tall, one leaning on a cane. Not everything that puts a person on a cane is a choice, but a great deal of what keeps you off one is a weekly pattern, and that is a choice. The number behind the picture: in 183 countries, the gap between how long people live and how long they live well is 9.6 years; in the United States it is 12.4, the widest in the world. Twelve years, at the end, in poor health. Those twelve years are what this layer is about.

THE ONE IDEA

Same birthday, different last twelve years. The weekly pattern is the difference.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

A true split screen, one frame, same light, same background, two women of the same age. On the left she is mid-movement, a real woman doing a real lift, upright and strong. On the right the same-aged woman leans on a cane. Two words, cream, centered low: Same age. Then, under each figure, two bars: years lived, and years lived well, and the 12.4-year gap shown as the red difference under the woman on the right. The photograph makes the room feel it; the bars make it a number they cannot argue with.

BUILT WITH

One split photograph, authentic, no overlays on the people; the bars drawn beneath. Garmany and Terzic, Mayo Clinic, JAMA Network Open 2024.

slides.title: Four types of movement, four parts of you.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 12 · 3:30
Four types of movement, four parts of you.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Movement is a portfolio; everything in one stock is not diversified, it is optimistic. Four tiles. Weights, resistance against a load, compound lifts: for bones and muscle. VO2 max, how much oxygen the body can use when working hard: for the heart. Zone 2, easy cardio at a conversational pace: for the heart. Mobility and balance, the tile everybody forgets: for the brain as much as the body, and the one that keeps you doing the other three. Each tile has a number researchers use to predict how long you live: grip strength, fitness, steps a day, the one-leg stand. Seven thousand steps, not ten. Try the one-leg stand tonight.

THE ONE IDEA

Four kinds of movement, each feeding a different part of you, each with a number that predicts your life.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

The body map: one translucent figure in profile, realistic, not neon, with four points that light as she names them: bones and muscle, heart, heart, brain. Around the figure, four tiles, and each tile is a real picture of the movement, a woman under a bar, a woman on a bike at full effort, a woman walking at a talking pace, a woman standing on one leg, with a line from the tile to the part of the body it serves and the predictor number beside it: grip strength, fitness, 7,000 steps, the one-leg stand. The slide shows the exercise and what it does inside the body on one screen, which is the only way a room of five hundred understands "four parts of you".

BUILT WITH

The figure rendered as a medical-illustration body, the four exercise pictures photographed, the lines and numbers drawn. López-Bueno et al., 2022; Lang et al., BJSM 2024; Ding et al., Lancet Public Health 2025; Araujo et al., BJSM 2022; Mayo Clinic, PLOS One 2024.

slides.title: What my week looks like.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 13 · 1:30
What my week looks like.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Three strength sessions on compound lifts, two zone-2 sessions, one sprint-interval session, an eight-thousand-step floor every day. More than anyone needs on day one; begin where you are. A walk after the biggest meal earns its place.

THE ONE IDEA

The portfolio, placed on seven days. This is what diversified looks like.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

Seven blocks, Monday to Sunday, each colored by its type in the same four colors as the tiles on the previous slide, so the room sees the portfolio land on a calendar. One thin line runs under all seven: the eight-thousand-step floor. No text beyond the day and the type. It is the drill-down after the macro slide, and it is deliberately the simplest object in the deck.

BUILT WITH

Seven blocks drawn, the step line beneath. Her current template to confirm, and where mobility and balance sit.

slides.title: The layer people skip.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 14 · 5:00
The layer people skip.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Stress, the layer people skip, and the one she found out was real the hard way: a divorce, a test, cortisol high. Stress hormones are built for short bursts; when they never switch off they wear the body down. She found a transcendental meditation center, learned it, and six months later her cortisol was normal and stayed there. Not a promise; the best practice is the one you will do. Then the free tool: the physiological sigh, tested at Stanford on 111 people, five minutes a day for a month. Two short inhales through the nose, one long exhale through the mouth. Three together, on camera.

THE ONE IDEA

Stress is a number that can come down, and the cheapest tool for it takes thirty seconds.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

The cake with stress lit, held through her story, with no graph and no numbers, because the story is personal and the screen should stay out of the way. Then the breath: two short arcs rising, one long arc falling, drawn large and animating at speaking pace as she leads the room through it. The arcs are the instruction; the room breathes with the line on the screen.

BUILT WITH

The cake photograph with the stress layer lit; the breath arcs drawn and animated. Balban, Spiegel and Huberman, Cell Reports Medicine 2023.

slides.title: Julie Gibson Clark's Longevity Protocol
slides.notes:
SLIDE 15 · 5:30
Julie Gibson Clark's Longevity Protocol
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Her day, so the room sees where the layers fit and where they fight for the same hour. Five, wake, water, light. Seven, training, then the sauna. Eight, eating window opens. Ten, coffee cuts off. The ten-hour window is not an accident: the Salk trial in 2024 improved HbA1c and body fat inside an eight-to-ten-hour window. Midday, the biggest meal, then a walk. Afternoon, meditation. Six, last meal. Eight, screens off. Nine, lights out. If you squint, the day is built backward from bedtime. And the honest part: a nine o'clock bedtime fights with a family dinner at 7:30 and a good glass of wine. Screenshot this slide; it is the page they were promised.

THE ONE IDEA

Her whole protocol is one day, and the day is built backward from bedtime.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

The day ring: her day as a clock, 5 AM to 9 PM, 9 PM at the top so the eye starts at bedtime. Every hour colored by its layer: blue for sleep and the wind-down, amber for movement and the sauna, green for the eating window, lavender for meditation. The ten hours from eight to six shaded as one band. Large hour marks for the nine moments she names. Two small collision marks where her day fights the world: the 7:30 dinner, the glass of wine. The kicker above the headline reads "the day is built backward from bedtime", so the sentence is on the slide when she says it. This is the one slide built to be screenshotted, so it is the cleanest object in the hour.

BUILT WITH

The ring drawn, with the hour list beside it in her words. Manoogian et al., Annals of Internal Medicine 2024, the TIMET trial.

slides.title: Test. Then buy.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 16 · 7:30
Test. Then buy.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

People think measuring is the expensive part; it is not. Every layer shows up in a number you can get without a lab; a notebook and a cheap watch tell you most of it. Then supplements, kept short on purpose: her list is for her body and her tests. Work with your doctor to find what you are short on: vitamin D, homocysteine, red blood cell nutrient levels. Test first, then decide what to buy; a supplement is icing and a test tells you where the cake has a hole. Her list, as what one person chose, with the NOVOS disclosure. Inside the Academy a whole session is spent on this with your own blood work.

THE ONE IDEA

Measure before you spend. The test finds the hole in the cake; the supplement fills it.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

Opens on an open notebook with the cake small beside it and the line "You don't need a lab. You need a notebook." Second build: the headline, and three tall cards: Vitamin D, Homocysteine, Red blood cell nutrient levels, one line beneath, "Ask your doctor which of these makes sense for you." Final build: the cards slide left and her list stands on its own, each item with its monthly cost and one total, the NOVOS disclosure in small type, under two words: "What one person chose." The list is shown as a list because she promised it, and shown last because the order is the lesson.

BUILT WITH

The notebook photographed; the cards and the list drawn. Her list and costs from her website, to confirm.

SLIDE 17 · 5:00
Why. Intention. Resources.
WHAT SHE IS SAYING

Numbers are not what kept her doing this for ten years; three questions did. What's my why: a kid who needs his mom to show up for a long time; a why is a direction. What's my intention: the sentence on the wall, "I want my healthspan to match my lifespan"; Fries drew it as two lines, how long you live and how long you live well, and the Mayo Clinic measured the gap, more than twelve years in this country; the point is to drag the second line up to meet the first. What are my resources: an hour in the morning and twelve dollars a day; resources set the pace. It is a circle, not a list: take one away and the other two fall over. Then the Blueprint, for people who have the time and the money and not someone to hold the plan. Then the ask: three lines and one thing in forty-eight hours.

THE ONE IDEA

Three questions hold each other up. Answer them once and they do the work every morning.

ON SCREEN, AND WHY

The closing cake, every layer lit, the white cake she would actually bake, whole with one slice lifted so the room sees all six layers one last time. Second build: two curves on one chart, how long we live and how long we live well, the gap between them, and the second line rising to close it, because that is her intention drawn as Fries drew it. Third build: the cake recedes and the ring of three rises, Why, Intention, Resources, a line between each pair, the center lighting only when all three are on, because that is her sentence about the circle. Fourth build: the Blueprint card in her video-card style, "The same cake, built week by week," in cream, "with a teacher." in light blue. Final: her ask, three lines and one thing.

BUILT WITH

The white cake photographed; the two curves drawn; the ring drawn; the Blueprint card in the card style from her videos. Fries, NEJM 1980; Garmany and Terzic, JAMA Network Open 2024.
